title: Over the Draw to the North Side
premise: Cross the town's first drawbridge into the North Side and see what stood on the far bank: a brickyard, the first house built for a school and a brick hotel going up. Nothing to count or carry.

opening.text:
JAUNT: OVER THE DRAW TO THE NORTH SIDE. An autumn afternoon. Most of the town's trade is on the south bank, but the North Side is where the money is going to live: by 1836 'The greater portion of the families of wealth, education and high social position' lived there, and the new Lake House was their 'fashionable headquarters'.

Cross the town's first drawbridge and watch the North Side being made: a brickyard, the first house ever built for a school, and a brick hotel going up.

stops.text: Start at the foot of Dearborn Street, at the town's first drawbridge, built in 1834 by the ship-carpenter Nelson R. Norton. Moses and Kirkland make it '300 feet in length, by sixteen in width', with 'a double draw'; Andreas gives a sixty-foot opening for craft and gallows frames at either end. When a schooner comes up the river, the draw goes up and everyone waits. Cross to the north bank.

Off the draw and a short way west along the bank, where Andreas puts Tyler K. Blodgett's brickyard of spring 1833, between Dearborn and Clark, with Henry S. Lampman the town's first brickmaker. The first brick building outside the fort went up that year, for John Noble, on the lot next to where the Lake House now rises. One drying shed stands for the whole yard.

A few steps on, just east of Clark Street, Andreas says Hamilton and Owen built a school-house in 1833, the first house built for a school in Chicago, and that in 1835 John Watkins taught the North Side's public school here. Watkins himself did not remember the building, which happens in a town that changes this fast. His first class, in 1832, met 'in a log house about twelve feet square', with twelve pupils.

East along the bank to Rush Street and the Lake House. Andreas describes the finished hotel: brick, three storeys and a basement, opened in autumn 1836. It 'aimed to cater for only the highest class of guests', and it will be the North Side's 'fashionable headquarters, where were given select parties'. For now it is walls and scaffolding. Choose how to end the outing.

choices.label: End at the Lake House site
choices.consequence: Finish on the North Side, at the corner of Rush Street.

choices.label: Back over the draw
choices.consequence: West along the bank and over the Dearborn Street draw to where you began.

stops.narrative: A hotel going up, and a choice of where to stop.

legs.note: Over the draw to the north bank and a short way west toward Clark Street, about 0.12 km.
legs.story: Across the river to the North Side.

legs.note: A few steps west along the bank, about 20 m; both places are the records' placements.
legs.story: From the yard to the school-house.

legs.note: East along the north bank to Rush Street, about 0.5 km.
legs.story: Along the bank to the building going up.

endings.text: You end the outing on the North Side, at the Lake House by Rush Street, having crossed by the draw and seen a brickyard, a school-house and the town's grandest hotel going up. In a year this will be the best address in Chicago.
You walk back west along the bank and over the Dearborn Street draw to South Water Street, where the outing began. Behind you the North Side is filling in, one brick at a time.

keepsake.title: North of the River
keepsake.text: A fictional note of a crossing by the Dearborn Street draw to a brickyard, a school-house and a hotel site on the far bank.

evidence.text: Nelson R. Norton, a ship-carpenter, writes in a letter Andreas prints that he cut the lumber for a drawbridge over the winter of 1833-34 and began building it in March 1834; Andreas notes the Democrat has it formally accepted by the Trustees in August. It was the first drawbridge across the river.
evidence.locator: Andreas vol. 1, the bridges section, Norton's letter beginning 'I came to Chicago November 16, 1833' and Andreas's correction 'Mr. Norton is evidently in error as to the time of the completion of the bridge'; with 'The first drawbridge thrown across the river was at Dearborn Street'. Read in the chicagology Dearborn Street bridges transcription.

evidence.text: Andreas: 'From various sources it is learned that it was about three hundred feet long, and the opening for the passage of craft about sixty feet.' It was of the 'gallows pattern', with frames one at either end of the draw.
evidence.locator: Andreas vol. 1, scan p. 415 (per docs/research/04-structures-south.md section 4), the paragraph on the Dearborn Street drawbridge, read verbatim in the chicagology Dearborn Street bridges transcription.

evidence.text: The bridge crosses the main stem in line with Dearborn Street, its south abutment at the foot of Dearborn on South Water Street.
evidence.reasoning: Follows the structure record dearborn_street_drawbridge, which places the crossing on the street it is named for and grades the position inferred. The jaunt starts at the south end; the crossing is the route's and claims no dated passage over the draw.

evidence.text: Andreas: in the spring of 1833 Tyler K. Blodgett established a brick-yard on the North Side, not far from the river bank, between Dearborn and Clark streets, and engaged Henry S. Lampman, then of Ann Arbor, as a workman; Lampman was undoubtedly the first brick-maker.
evidence.locator: Andreas vol. 1, scan p. 1161, the brick-making paragraph beginning 'In the spring of 1833, Tyler K. Blodgett established a brick-yard'.

evidence.text: The yard's shed is placed midway between the lines of Clark and Dearborn streets, about 17 m back from the traced north bank; the sentence bounds the block and the spot within it is the record's choice.
evidence.reasoning: Follows the structure record brickyard_north_side, which grades the position inferred from Andreas's locating sentence. The yard is an area and the scene draws one drying shed for it; the clamp, pit and hacks are recorded and not built, as the stop says.

evidence.text: That the yard was still worked on 1 July 1835 is inference: the Lake House going up in brick on the same bank is the best reason to think somebody was making brick in the town, and nothing says who.
evidence.reasoning: The structure record carries the yard's range to 1835 as inference from the town's brick building and says whether Blodgett was still on this ground is not attested; the stop says who worked it in July 1835 is not recorded, and does not say the Lake House's brick came from here.

evidence.text: Andreas reports from Mr. Wells's report that Hamilton and Owen built a house on the north bank of the river, just east of Clark Street, in which Watkins continued his school, the first house built for a school in Chicago, but adds that this does not recur to Watkins's recollection.
evidence.locator: Vol. 1, the schools chapter, the paragraph citing Mr. Wells's report (as quoted in data/structures/north_side_school_1833.json and docs/RESEARCH/north_side_school_1833.md § 1).

evidence.text: Andreas says that in 1835 John Watkins was teaching what had become a public school on the North Side, on the river bank just east of Clark Street, in the building Hamilton and Owen erected in 1833, and that the exact date of his retirement is not known.
evidence.locator: Vol. 1, the schools chapter, the 1835 paragraph following George Davis's school in the Presbyterian church (archive.org scan p. 433, as read in docs/research/04-structures-south.md § 9).

evidence.text: The school-house is placed on the North Water Street frontage just east of Clark; Andreas's Methodist chapter puts 'the Watkins school-house' between Clark and LaSalle, about a block west.
evidence.reasoning: The schools chapter's 'just east of Clark Street' is adopted because it is the more specific statement, made twice, in the chapter about the building; the structure record keeps the other reading as a stated uncertainty, so the stop speaks of the bank and the year, not a door or a July class.

evidence.text: Andreas: Chicago had a really grand hotel as early as 1835, the Lake House, at the corners of Kinzie, Rush and Michigan streets, fronting on the latter; built of brick, three stories and a basement in height; completed and thrown open to the public in the autumn of 1836.
evidence.locator: Andreas vol. 1, the hotels paragraph beginning 'Chicago did, however, have a really grand hotel as early as 1835', as transcribed under the heading 'Andreas' History of Chicago Volume I' on chicagology prefire112 (accessed 2026-08-11).

evidence.text: An uncredited modern paragraph says ground was broken for the Lake House in 1835; Andreas gives no groundbreaking, and this project grades the paragraph as its weakest kind of source.
evidence.locator: Chicagology prefire112, the uncredited paragraph beginning 'The Lake House hotel on the north side of the river', immediately after the Andreas paragraph (accessed 2026-08-11).

evidence.text: The first drawbridge, at Dearborn Street, built in 1834 with Nelson R. Norton as contractor, 'was 300 feet in length, by sixteen in width, and had a double draw'.
evidence.locator: p. 95, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 12811-12817 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: In 1833 about 165 frame buildings went up, and one of brick, 'the first in the town outside the fort', built by Alanson Sweet and William Worthingham for John Noble on a lot next to the one the Lake House later took.
evidence.locator: p. 90, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 12240-12258 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: Before the Lake House was finished, the first Unitarian service in Chicago was held in it, conducted by the Rev. Dr. Follen, with Harriet Martineau in the congregation; the inn 'aimed to cater for only the highest class of guests'.
evidence.locator: p. 561, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 98826-98837 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: 'The greater portion of the families of wealth, education and high social position in 1836 resided on the north side', and the Lake House, 'the first hotel constructed of brick', was 'the fashionable headquarters, where were given select parties'.
evidence.locator: p. 101, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 13538-13549 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: In the fall of 1832 John Watkins, from New York, was employed to teach a subscription school on the North Side 'in a log house about twelve feet square'; in his first quarter he had only twelve pupils.
evidence.locator: p. 90, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 12159-12164 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: On 1 July 1835 the scene draws the Lake House as a roofless brick shell one storey high, on the east side of Rush Street; the storey count, the plan and the side of the street are not documented.
evidence.reasoning: Follows the structure record lake_house_construction and its liberty: a building finished in autumn 1836 and begun, on the compilations, in 1835 is a building site on the scene date, and the record reasons one storey from the build schedule and grades it conjectural. The stop calls the shell our reconstruction and offers an exterior look only.

evidence.text: The outing, the crossing, the route order, the looking from the street, the choice of where to end, both endings, the timing inputs and the North of the River keepsake are invented connective narrative. No passage over the draw on a given day, no bridge-tender, brickmaker, teacher, pupil or builder is documented here, no interior is opened and no named person is met.
